items.title: Hafta letters: Questioning the ECI and Anand’s ‘institutional deference’
items.summary: Eveleen A bit disturbed by Anand’s use of the word ‘dramatic’ to describe how disenfranchised people have responded to the investigative report on the CEC (Chief Election Commissioner). I would like to bring your attention to the mediation of any social or political process by algorithms. It depoliticises a disenfranchising process and makes it look like a technical issue, even though the ECI has, by default, become the basis for defining citizenship. Perhaps that is why the response of disenfranchised and displaced people (if you go by Reporters’ Collective ) appears dramatic. The CEC is hiding behind an algorithm, and they are promising some amount of transparency. But can more surveillance be the solution to surveillance when the demand is for accountability and justice? These questions may “appear” dramatic in the face of an algorithm assembled by people. But when the violence is systemic, repetitive and based on systematic exclusion, voicing these questions should be obvious? *** Srinath I’d love to see an episode in the spirit of NPR’s Throughline that takes a step back from the current news cycle and examines, historically and institutionally, how the Modi government has altered India’s electoral democracy over the past 12 years – from electoral bonds and political-financing rules, to the appointment of Election Commissioners, to the recent Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. I’d also love a more sceptical examination of the Election Commission. At times, Anand’s institutional deference seems to me to border on apologism, even when serious questions about its conduct and independence deserve scrutiny. items.title: Supreme Court cancels Shiv Sena corporator Ramesh Mhatre’s bail in doctors' assault case
items.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday cancelled the bail granted to Shiv Sena corporator Ramesh Mhatre in a case concerning the alleged assault on doctors and hospital staff in Dombivli [ State of Maharashtra v. Ramesh Sukrya Mhatre ]. A Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta set aside a Bombay High Court order which had allowed Mhatre's release. The Bench observed that a firm signal needed to be sent against attacks on healthcare professionals. It also refused to fix any timeline for the completion of the trial. "The message must go loud and clear! Medical fraternity cannot be touched. Just see the brazen nature of these people. Even after this incident, there have been other incidents related to the same party. Medical fraternity serves people. They can’t be touched and attacked in this manner," the Court orally remarked during the hearing. It then directed Mhatre to surrender within 3 days. Justice Vikram Nath and Justice Sandeep Mehta In its judgment, the Court also commented extensively on the need to protect doctors while performing their duties, including by quoting from the Sanskrit treatise on medicine, Suśruta Saṃhitā. "(The Suśruta Saṃhitā says) physician does not succeed in a house where he is not respected; where the physician is respected, his treatment succeeds .... A doctor cannot reasonably be expected to exercise sound and independent judgment while labouring under the apprehension of physical violence, intimidation or coercion. The safety and dignity of the medical professional are consequently not matters of personal privilege. They are the safeguards which serve the larger public interest in ensuring that medical care is rendered with the concentration, composure and judgment that the profession demands," the Court observed. The Court clarified that it is not stating that doctors are beyond legal scrutiny, but that any complaints about a doctors' treatment of patients must be made through appropriate, legal channels. "What the law cannot countenance is the substitution of these remedies by threat, violence and coercion. Physical violence, intimidation or coercion cannot become a means of expressing dissatisfaction with medical treatment, securing compliance with a demand or raising grievance for an adverse medical outcome. A grievance, however genuine, does not confer a licence to resort to violence," the Court warned.
